name: Venetic
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Lejeune, Michel. 1974. Manuel de la langue vénète. Heidelberg: Carl Winter Universitätsverlag (ISBN 3 533 02353 2). 341 pp.
catalog_quote: 181. Accent. Nous n'avons d'autre information que celle qu'on peut inférer des syncopes de voyelles brèves, lesquelles sont de date historique, et ne jouent dans l'histoire de la langue qu'un rôle mineur (ch. VII B). Leur distribution fait penser à un relief particulier de la syllabe initiale; peut-être les composés dont le premier terme est disyllabique comportaient-ils un double relief accentuel, au niveau des initiales des deux termes. [p. 159] ... 133. L'affaiblissement des voyelles brèves en seconde syllabe (très différent, dans ses modalités, des syncopes intérieures du latin et de celles que présente, bien plus largement, l'osco-ombrien), témoigne, comme l'affaiblissement des voyelles brèves en syllabe finale, d'un relief particulier de la syllabe initiale. Si la majorité de nos exemples concerne des composés ou des syntagmes prépositionnels, c'est sans doute que la seconde syllabe se trouvait alors à la fois précédée et suivie d'une syllabe en relief: ekvŏ-petāri-, upŏ-sedo-, opĭ-tergyo-, *opĭ yŏrobos, *vantŏ-keno-, etc. [p. 125]

new_statements.translation: 181. Accent. We have no information other than what can be inferred from the syncopes of short vowels, which are of historical date and play only a minor role in the history of the language (ch. VII B). Their distribution suggests a particular prominence of the initial syllable; perhaps compounds whose first member is disyllabic had a double accentual prominence, on the initial syllables of both members.

new_statements.locator: Ch. 'Le mot phonétique', §181 'Accent', p. 159 (PDF page 157 of the archive.org scan); supporting §133, p. 125 (§§ 132-134 'Syncopes de brèves')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (342 pp., Acrobat text) with extracted text and the companion. PDF page 157 carries the running head '§§ 181-183 LE MOT PHONÉTIQUE 159' and the passage '181. Accent. Nous n'avons d'autre information que celle qu'on peut inférer des syncopes de voyelles brèves, lesquelles sont de date historique, et ne jouent dans l'histoire de la langue qu'un rôle mineur (ch. VII B). Leur distribution fait penser à un relief particulier de la syllabe initiale; peut-être les composés dont le premier terme est disyllabique comportaient-ils un double relief accentuel, au niveau des initiales des deux termes.' ( lines 8730-8738) -- word-for-word identical to the reported quote. §182 'Rythme quantitatif'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (a prominence inferred only from the pattern of short-vowel syncope in second and final syllables) fell on the initial syllable of the word. Lejeune §133 (p. 125) states the same inference: the weakening of short vowels in the second syllable and in the final syllable 'témoigne.. d'un relief particulier de la syllabe initiale'. No direct evidence (metrical texts, orthographic marking) exists; §182 adds that word rhythm was plausibly quantitative but cannot be demonstrated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Possibly a second prominence on the initial syllable of the second member of compounds whose first member is disyllabic ('double relief accentuel, au niveau des initiales des deux termes'), i.e. ekvó-petári-, upó-sedo-, opi-tergyo- type (§133).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author stresses that the only evidence is syncope of historical date, so the statement is an inference, not an observation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, inferred from inscriptional orthography of an extinct language; no citation forms or phrase-level information. Wallace 2008 (snippet) restates it second-hand as 'a stress accent system with stress positioned on or near the initial syllable (Lejeune 1974:125; Prosdocimi 1978:318)'; Beeler 1949: 42-43 had earlier argued that nothing can be said about the position or nature of the Venetic accent because he rejected the evidence for medial syncope.
new_statements.identity_note: Venetic (vene1257, ISO xve) is an extinct fragmentary IE language known only from c. 300+ inscriptions (Este, Padova, Vicenza, Lagole/Cadore, Trieste area). Lejeune's statement concerns the language as a whole, not a dialect; all accent claims in the literature are inferences from syncope patterns in the orthography, never direct observation. The Lejeune 1974 file is a user upload on archive.org (folkscanomy, by A. R. Bomhard) of an in-copyright 1974 Carl Winter book; a controlled-lending copy (manueldelalangue0000leje) also exists there.

sources.quote: Now it would seem that if Venetic preserved so faithfully the position of the Indo-European accent, it might be expected that the Indo-European nature of that accent would have been kept -- that it would have been a pitch and not a stress accent. And if it had had a pitch accent we should expect the full preservation of the vowels of unaccented syllables, as in Greek, which is what we seem to have in Venetic, if the examples quoted above were rightly interpreted. But we can, of course, say nothing about either the position or the nature of Venetic accent from the fact that its medial vowels are preserved; for the preservation of medial and final short vowels and of the original diphthongs is a marked feature of the oldest Latin, even though that language presumably had already at that the first reading strong initial stress accent. Hence I can see no reason for Conway's "a priori probability" of syncope, and must therefore examine the examples which are adduced to support it.
sources.locator: pp. 42-43, section V.3 'The Evidence for Vowel Syncope in Venetic'; conclusion p. 44 (PDF 52): 'But there are no certain examples within Venetic itself.'
sources.note: Beeler states no accent system: he holds that the position and nature of the Venetic accent cannot be determined from the inscriptions. sources.note: §3 'The Evidence for Vowel Syncope in Venetic', pp. 42-44: rejects Conway's claim of medial syncope and Conway's theory that the puncts mark word accent; concludes 'we can, of course, say nothing about either the position or the nature of Venetic accent from the fact that its medial vowels are preserved' (pp. 42-43); allows that syncope 'may have begun to take place at the end of the Venetic period' (p. 43). Earlier (p. 9 area) lists Conway's accent theory of the puncts among rejected explanations.
